title: Mistake, impracticability, and frustration: editorial notes and questions
summary: Read the surrounding notes and questions alongside the principal cases. The complete assigned pages are preserved here.
notes:
Stees v. Leonard: Stees establishes the background expectation that a party bears the risks its promise allocates. It connects the definition of the promised result, parol evidence, modification, and excuse.

Renner v. Kehl: Renner distinguishes avoiding a contract from obtaining damages for its breach. The legal basis of relief determines which losses and benefits enter the calculation.

Taylor v. Caldwell: Taylor identifies a limited setting in which an unexpected event destroys an essential basis of performance, rather than merely making the promised work more costly.

Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States: The case teaches the sequence for evaluating changed circumstances and the difference between predicting a risk, allocating it, and proving that it made performance impracticable.

Krell v. Henry: Krell explains why a contract can be excused even where performing it remains possible: the shared, particular purpose for receiving the performance may have disappeared.
